claims.text: The target specimen is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing exactly 1 wt.% oxygen.
Oxygen is uniformly distributed as defects throughout the alloy.
The alloy has a high-entropy disordered crystalline matrix.
A physics-informed machine-learning model combined with EMT parameters will predict conductivity with less than 10% error over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The hybrid model will outperform conventional defect-free analytical models.
Experimental conductivity datasets spanning 0–200 K and 300–1200 K are available for model training or calibration.
EMT-derived oxygen-scattering factors, defect density, and lattice-distortion indicators can represent defect-induced and phonon-induced scattering.
Electrical transport from 0–200 K is dominated by defect scattering.
Electrical transport from 300–1200 K is dominated by phonon scattering.
Measurements or calibration points exist near 50 K, 400 K, 750 K, and 1000 K for specimens containing precisely 1 wt.% oxygen.
Physics-informed constraints on the integrated descriptor vector will guide the machine-learning model.
Oxygen-induced defect scattering dominates conductivity at low temperatures.
At higher temperatures, phonon scattering and oxygen-related effects both contribute significantly to conductivity.
Embedding experimentally calibrated physical parameters mitigates the oversimplification of defect-free analytical models.
Perfect-crystal analytical models typically neglect oxygen-induced defect scattering.
Neglecting oxygen-induced defect scattering causes systematic prediction inaccuracies across the specified temperature ranges.
The proposed applicability is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing controlled 1 wt.% oxygen and to 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
A prediction error greater than 15% at a held-out 750 K benchmark will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The 750 K point is described as a calibration point but is also designated as the held-out benchmark. A point used for calibration cannot simultaneously provide an independent held-out test unless a separate 750 K specimen or dataset is explicitly reserved.

The central prediction requires error below or within 10%, whereas falsification requires error greater than 15%. Errors between 10% and 15% violate the stated prediction but would not trigger the stated rejection rule.
